Laser Treatment for Scars

How Scar Lasers Work and Who They Help　When to Start and How Many Sessions?

Division of General Plastic Surgery · S.H. Kwon, MD Patient Education Patients & Families

After an injury, a burn, or surgery, many people worry about being left with a noticeable scar. What should you do if, after the wound has healed, the scar gradually turns red and raised, or becomes itchy, painful, or tight?

With advances in medical technology, laser treatment has become one of the important options for treating scars. Besides improving appearance, it can also help relieve the discomfort that scars cause.

How Soon After a Wound Heals Can Laser Treatment Begin?

It used to be commonly believed that a scar had to wait six months to a year, until it was fully mature, before it could be treated with a laser. However, recent studies have found that for some scars, laser treatment started early after the wound has healed may help reduce scar overgrowth and improve the scar's later appearance.

In general, once the wound has completely healed, with no broken skin, oozing, or infection, a doctor can assess whether laser treatment can begin.

For some patients, early laser treatment can be considered about 2–4 weeks after the wound has healed; it is not always necessary to wait six months or a year.

Is Earlier Always Better?

Early treatment may help, but earlier is not always better.

A scar keeps changing after the wound has healed. Burn scars in particular may gradually thicken and harden over several months. Appropriate early laser treatment may help reduce scar overgrowth.

However, if the wound has not fully healed, is still infected, or the skin is too fragile, treating too early may instead cause new damage.

So what matters is not how many days after healing the laser is started, but the doctor's assessment of whether the wound is stable, how the scar is changing, and which type of laser is suitable.

What Types of Scar Lasers Are There?

There are currently two main types of laser commonly used for scars:

Pulsed Dye Laser (PDL)

Mainly improves: scar redness and increased blood vessels.

This type of laser acts mainly on the blood vessels within the scar. It can improve scar redness and may also relieve some itching and early scar overgrowth. It is suited to scars that remain noticeably red after the wound has healed.

Fractional CO₂ Laser

Mainly improves: scar thickening, stiffness, unevenness, and tightness.

It creates tiny treatment zones within the scar tissue, encouraging the collagen to rearrange and improving the scar's thickness, softness, and skin texture. It may give good improvement for hypertrophic scars after burns, or for scars that make the skin feel tight. Some patients can also combine the two lasers to address different scar problems.

How Many Sessions Are Needed?

Scar laser treatment usually requires multiple sessions, commonly about 3–5 or more; the actual number depends on how severe the scar is and how it responds to treatment.

Typical treatment intervals are:

  • Pulsed dye laser: about once every 4–6 weeks.
  • Fractional CO₂ laser: about once every 6–12 weeks.

After treatment, scars usually become gradually flatter and softer, and their color may also improve.

It is important to note that the goal of laser treatment is to improve the scar, not to make it disappear completely.

Can Children Have Scar Laser Treatment?

Yes. Being a child is not a reason to rule out scar laser treatment.

Children are still growing and developing. If a scar from a burn or other injury keeps thickening or contracting (contracture), it may affect joint movement and normal development.

For this reason, children with significant scar overgrowth, itching, pain, or limited movement can be evaluated by a specialist early.

During treatment, the doctor will choose an appropriate method of pain relief or anesthesia based on the child's age, the size of the scarred area, and how well the child can cooperate. Some children can use a topical anesthetic cream, while younger children or those with larger treatment areas may need to be assessed for sedation or general anesthesia.

What Should I Watch for After Laser Treatment?

After laser treatment, there may be temporary redness and swelling, bruising, or scabbing, which usually resolve gradually.

After treatment, keep the skin moisturized and protected from the sun, care for the treated area as instructed by your doctor, and avoid picking off the scabs.

In addition, scar treatment does not rely on laser alone. It still needs to be combined with silicone gel, pressure garments, medication injections, or rehabilitation therapy to achieve better results.

Conclusion

Scar laser treatment does more than improve appearance; it can also help relieve itching, pain, and tightness. A scar does not have to be fully mature before treatment begins, but earlier is not always better. With a professional assessment and the right choice of treatment timing and laser type, scars can be improved safely.

If, after the wound has healed, the scar stays red, raised, or itchy, or limits your movement, it is advisable to have it evaluated early at a plastic surgery or scar clinic.

This article provides general health information and does not replace individual medical advice. Actual treatment must be decided after an in-person evaluation.

Written by S.H. Kwon, MD, Division of General Plastic Surgery, Linkou Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (translated from the Chinese original)
